ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Fifty-seven able-bodied participants completed an object repositioning task over an obstacle with prosthetic avatars that varied in motor autonomy and appearance.
Participants were recruited across two data acquisition rounds.
Participants were compensated either with 25 CHF or two student participation credits.
Data were collected from seventy-four participants.

From these, seventeen participants were later excluded from the final analysis: twelve due to incomplete data files caused by technical problems during acquisition, four due to a lack of understanding or not following the instructions, and one after it was observed that the participant did not meet the inclusion criteria post-acquisition.
Afterwards, the participants were fitted with the VR headset, and the eye-tracker was individually calibrated.
Before starting the task, participants were introduced to the VR environments and the virtual prostheses they would use to become familiar with them.
The experimental blocks 24 trials with sound delays of 200, 400, and 600 milliseconds, and participants were asked for their time estimation of the delay and their sense of agency over it.

Since participants were not told about this manipulation, all five delay options (1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds) were available, allowing participants to select the one they perceived as appropriate if their temporal perception was influenced by the intentional binding effect.

The participants had to reposition the cylinder themselves in every experimental block, except in the passive condition, where the cylinder moved autonomously when the white button was pressed at the beginning of each trial.
Following the completion of each of the five experimental blocks, participants were directed to look at the virtual avatar of their arm for 30 seconds, during which they could move it and operate it.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

> Fifty-seven able-bodied participants completed an object repositioning task over an obstacle with prosthetic avatars that varied in motor autonomy and appearance.

> Participants were recruited across two data acquisition rounds.

> Participants were compensated either with 25 CHF or two student participation credits.

> Data were collected from seventy-four participants.

> From these, seventeen participants were later excluded from the final analysis: twelve due to incomplete data files caused by technical problems during acquisition, four due to a lack of understanding or not following the instructions, and one after it was observed that the participant did not meet the inclusion criteria post-acquisition.

> Afterwards, the participants were fitted with the VR headset, and the eye-tracker was individually calibrated.

> Before starting the task, participants were introduced to the VR environments and the virtual prostheses they would use to become familiar with them.

> The experimental blocks 24 trials with sound delays of 200, 400, and 600 milliseconds, and participants were asked for their time estimation of the delay and their sense of agency over it.

> Since participants were not told about this manipulation, all five delay options (1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds) were available, allowing participants to select the one they perceived as appropriate if their temporal perception was influenced by the intentional binding effect.

> The participants had to reposition the cylinder themselves in every experimental block, except in the passive condition, where the cylinder moved autonomously when the white button was pressed at the beginning of each trial.

> Following the completion of each of the five experimental blocks, participants were directed to look at the virtual avatar of their arm for 30 seconds, during which they could move it and operate it.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: According to our power approximation, we aimed to collect at least fifty-three participants in order to detect a medium to large effect size f² =0.25, an α=0.05 for false positives, Power (1-β)=0.80 for the detection of a true effect, and four predictors in our most complex model. Data were collected from seventy-four participants. From these, seventeen participants were later excluded from the final analysis: twelve due to incomplete data files caused by technical problems during acquisition, four due to a lack of understanding or not following the instructions, and one after it was observed that the participant did not meet the inclusion criteria post-acquisition. Consequently, the final sample size comprised fifty-seven participants, with a mean age of 22.28 (SD = 2.79) years, including twenty self-reported males, thirty-six self-reported females, and one self-reported non-binary individual.

Using the condition HF as the reference level, no significant effect was found of aesthetic appearance on repositioning accuracy (β = -1.01, SE = 1.19, t(1264) = -0.85, p = .398).

The effect of motor autonomy showed a trend toward higher accuracy under the conditions with slippage compensation than in those without slippage compensation (β = 1.88, SE = 1.06, t(1266) = 1.77, p = .076).
The interaction between aesthetic appearance and motor autonomy was not significant (β = -1.61, SE = 1.52, t(1258) = -1.06, p = .290).

Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction showed significant differences in the repositioning accuracy in successful trials, with higher accuracy values in the HS condition than in the RF condition (mean difference = 2.89 percentage points, SE = 1.08, t(1256) = 2.68, p = .045).
In addition, accuracy was higher in the HS condition than in the RS condition (mean difference = 2.62 percentage points, SE = 0.96, t(1256) = 2.73, p = .038).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "In panel C, asterisks indicate significant differences from zero in the supplementary one-sample tests using available active-passive pairs at each delay (p < .05)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 1 data file could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

-  We assessed AND ran 2 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).

live_data_statements: Fifty-seven able-bodied participants completed an object repositioning task over an obstacle with prosthetic avatars that varied in motor autonomy and appearance.
Participants were recruited across two data acquisition rounds.
Participants were compensated either with 25 CHF or two student participation credits.
Data were collected from seventy-four participants.

From these, seventeen participants were later excluded from the final analysis: twelve due to incomplete data files caused by technical problems during acquisition, four due to a lack of understanding or not following the instructions, and one after it was observed that the participant did not meet the inclusion criteria post-acquisition.
Afterwards, the participants were fitted with the VR headset, and the eye-tracker was individually calibrated.
Before starting the task, participants were introduced to the VR environments and the virtual prostheses they would use to become familiar with them.
The experimental blocks 24 trials with sound delays of 200, 400, and 600 milliseconds, and participants were asked for their time estimation of the delay and their sense of agency over it.

Since participants were not told about this manipulation, all five delay options (1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds) were available, allowing participants to select the one they perceived as appropriate if their temporal perception was influenced by the intentional binding effect.

The participants had to reposition the cylinder themselves in every experimental block, except in the passive condition, where the cylinder moved autonomously when the white button was pressed at the beginning of each trial.
Following the completion of each of the five experimental blocks, participants were directed to look at the virtual avatar of their arm for 30 seconds, during which they could move it and operate it.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 2 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------

"02_Statistical_Analysis_V4_only48.R"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric")), row.names = c(NA, -2L
), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 2 scripts: 2 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("01_Statistical_Analysis_V4.R", "02_Statistical_Analysis_V4_only48.R"
), Outcome = c("ran_ok", "ran_ok"), Detail = c("", ""), "Time (s)" = c(36, 
35.3)), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: 01_Statistical_Analysis_V4.R, 02_Statistical_Analysis_V4_only48.R.

#### Reported vs. reproduced
91 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 1 matched (0 fully, 1 partially) — 1.1% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The "Plausible" column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output's own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.
reproducibility_check.checklist_section:
We ran the paper's 2 R scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script.

**2 of 2 scripts ran to the end**.

| Script | Result | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| 01_Statistical_Analysis_V4.R | Ran to the end |  |
| 02_Statistical_Analysis_V4_only48.R | Ran to the end |  |

### Other problems in the files

- 01_Statistical_Analysis_V4.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author's computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.
- 02_Statistical_Analysis_V4_only48.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author's computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

### Comparison with the paper

Of the 91 statistical tests reported in the paper, 1 was found in the output of the code.

text.text: Suffering a limb amputation has a major impact on physical and psychological health, with prosthetic devices being a fundamental tool to mitigate it.

Prosthesis embodiment (integrating a prosthetic device into the bodily self) is a fundamental process for accepting these devices, with the sense of agency (the experience of controlling one's actions and, through them, the course of external events) as a key contributing factor.
Current upper-limb myoelectric prostheses still present high abandonment rates, partly due to motor-control errors that may reduce the sense of agency associated with prosthesis movements.
One possible solution is sharing motor autonomy between the user and a grasping intention-detection algorithm, with prosthetic movements combining user actions and inferred intentions.

In this study, we investigated whether shared autonomy, simulated through automated grasp assistance by an idealised intention-detection system in immersive virtual reality, influences explicit (self-reported) and implicit (indirectly assessed) sense of agency, prosthesis embodiment, task performance, and gaze behaviour.
Fifty-seven able-bodied participants completed an object repositioning task over an obstacle with prosthetic avatars that varied in motor autonomy and appearance.
Shared autonomy increased self-reported agency and reduced failed attempts.
However, neither appearance nor motor autonomy affected embodiment scores.
Although explicit and implicit measures of agency were significantly correlated, they responded differently to experimental manipulations.
Shared autonomy increased explicit but not implicit agency, while longer actionoutcome delays were associated with reduced explicit agency but stronger intentional binding.
revealing dissociations across conditions and action-outcome delays.
Additionally, explicit agency was associated with reduced visual attention towards the prosthesis and manipulated object.

Together, these results indicate that shared autonomy approaches can enhance control experience and improve task performance while highlighting distinctions between explicit and implicit agency measures during prosthesis control.

The loss of an upper limb can have a profound impact on both the physical and psychological well-being of affected individuals, with the severity of these consequences generally increasing with the level of the amputation (Jo et al., 2021; Nedder et al., 2026).

text.text: Prostheses are commonly used as substitutes for missing limbs and are intended to enhance users' physical and psychological functioning and well-being (Caldas et al., 2026; Lathouwers et al., 2023).

text.text: For the acceptance of these artificial limbs, their integration into the user's bodily self becomes a fundamental aspect, which is referred to as prosthesis embodiment (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2021).

text.text: Prosthetic embodiment involves the integration of sensory, motor, and affective information through a prosthetic interface (De Vignemont, 2011; Makin et al., 2017; Saetta et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Prosthetic embodiment involves the integration of sensory, motor, and affective information through a prosthetic interface <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(De Vignemont, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Makin et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Saetta et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Current models propose that this process is mainly shaped by three interrelated aspects: sense of ownership/integrity, anatomical plausibility, and sense of agency associated with prosthesis movements (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2020).
text.formatted: Current models propose that this process is mainly shaped by three interrelated aspects: sense of ownership/integrity, anatomical plausibility, and sense of agency associated with prosthesis movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bekrater-Bodmann, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Sense of ownership refers to the feeling that one's body or body parts belong to oneself.

It is dependent on the integration of congruent sensory information with the body schema, a dynamic sensorimotor representation of the body's position and configuration (Tajadura-Jiménez et al., 2015; Tsakiris, 2010; Zbinden et al., 2022).
text.formatted: It is dependent on the integration of congruent sensory information with the body schema, a dynamic sensorimotor representation of the body's position and configuration <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Tajadura-Jiménez et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Tsakiris, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Zbinden et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Anatomical plausibility refers to how closely the prosthetic device matches the user's body schema in terms of perceived anatomy, position, orientation, and kinematics (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2021; Tsakiris, 2010; Tsakiris & Haggard, 2005).
text.formatted: Anatomical plausibility refers to how closely the prosthetic device matches the user's body schema in terms of perceived anatomy, position, orientation, and kinematics <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bekrater-Bodmann, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Tsakiris, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Tsakiris & Haggard, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, studies have found that aesthetic satisfaction with the prosthesis promotes prosthesis embodiment, with a general preference for a prosthesis that more closely resembles an intact limb (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2021; Caldas et al., 2026).

text.text: The sense of agency refers to the experience of controlling one's motor actions and, through them, the course of external events (Haggard, 2017).
text.formatted: The sense of agency refers to the experience of controlling one's motor actions and, through them, the course of external events <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Haggard, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This experience of the sense of agency can be measured either explicitly, through self-report by the individual, or implicitly, through phenomena like intentional binding (Caspar et al., 2015; Haggard, 2017; Haggard et al., 2002).
text.formatted: This experience of the sense of agency can be measured either explicitly, through self-report by the individual, or implicitly, through phenomena like intentional binding <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Caspar et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Haggard, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Haggard et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Intentional binding has been defined as the compression of the perceived temporal interval between a self-generated action and its consequence.

It can be assessed using different paradigms, including the Libet clock task, which measures the perceived timing of actions and outcomes (Haggard et al., 2002) and interval-estimation tasks, which involve either open-ended estimates (Engbert et al., 2007), or selection from a predetermined set of temporal intervals (Zapparoli et al., 2020).

text.text: Prostheses vary according to the body part they are intended to replace and whether their primary purpose is aesthetic or functional (Biddiss & Chau, 2007).
text.formatted: Prostheses vary according to the body part they are intended to replace and whether their primary purpose is aesthetic or functional <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Biddiss & Chau, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Functional upperlimb devices may be powered by body movements (body-powered), by external power sources while being controlled by the muscle activity of the stump (myoelectric), or a combination of both (hybrid) (Smail et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Functional upperlimb devices may be powered by body movements (body-powered), by external power sources while being controlled by the muscle activity of the stump (myoelectric), or a combination of both (hybrid) <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Smail et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Despite myoelectric prostheses offering more degrees of freedom than body-powered ones, acceptance remains low, with an estimated rejection rate of at least 20% in below-elbow amputations and 60% in aboveelbow amputations, favouring the use of body-powered or aesthetic alternatives instead (Salminger et al., 2022).

text.text: These low acceptance rates are associated with a reduced sense of embodiment and satisfaction with the device (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2021; Smail et al., 2020).

text.text: When a prosthesis is not successfully integrated into the user's body schema, its disadvantages, such as weight, cost, functional limitations, and maintenance requirements, may become more salient.
These factors are among the most frequently reported reasons for the rejection of these devices (Biddiss & Chau, 2007; Caldas et al., 2026; Smail et al., 2020).
text.formatted: These factors are among the most frequently reported reasons for the rejection of these devices <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Biddiss & Chau, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Caldas et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Smail et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Although the senses of ownership and agency can be dissociated, they may also reinforce each other (Braun et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Although the senses of ownership and agency can be dissociated, they may also reinforce each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Braun et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: One factor contributing to a reduced sense of embodiment may be a diminished sense of agency over the device.

In myoelectric prostheses, misclassifications of movements remain common, particularly in polyarticulated systems (Alotaibi et al., 2023), potentially reducing the association between the user's intended actions and the actual outcomes of their movements (Krugwasser et al., 2019; Salminger et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In myoelectric prostheses, misclassifications of movements remain common, particularly in polyarticulated systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alotaibi et al., 2023)</ref>, potentially reducing the association between the user's intended actions and the actual outcomes of their movements <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Krugwasser et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Salminger et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Shared-autonomy approaches have been proposed to address this challenge, in which control is distributed between the user and the prosthetic device.
By combining user actions with information about their inferred intentions, these systems may improve movement execution while maintaining or improving the user's sense of agency.

Consequently, shared autonomy may reduce control errors and misdetections while strengthening the correspondence between intended and observed actions, thereby potentially enhancing the user's sense of agency over the prosthesis.

In this study, we investigated whether shared autonomy, simulated through automated grasp assistance by an idealised intention-detection algorithm could influence the sense of agency and embodiment experienced over a virtual prosthesis in an immersive virtual reality (VR) environment, as a positive impact of these algorithms could improve the acceptance rate of prosthetic devices.
We also explored whether these effects were moderated by the external appearance of the prosthesis.
Additionally, we assessed the impact of the system motor control on performance during an object repositioning task to evaluate the potential functional benefits of shared autonomy.

Finally, we examined whether the strength of experienced sense of agency was associated with changes in visual attention toward the prosthesis, the manipulated object, and the goal location, to investigate whether gaze behaviour could provide complementary behavioural information about users' subjective experience while controlling the device.
We hypothesised that shared autonomy would increase the sense of agency over the prosthesis and improve task performance.
We further hypothesised that a stronger sense of agency would be associated with reduced visual attention toward the prosthesis, reflecting a reduced need to monitor its operation.

text.text: Participants were recruited across two data acquisition rounds.

The first round was conducted via the University Registration Center for Study Participants (UAST) platform, shared by the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich (ETHZ) and the University of Zurich (UZH), to recruit participants.
The second round was conducted through the SONA platform at the University of Konstanz.

Inclusion criteria included understanding English, being an adult (ages 18 to 65 years), being right-handed, not having a history of neurological and/or psychiatric disorders, and not suffering from orthopaedic conditions affecting the upper limbs.
Participants were compensated either with 25 CHF or two student participation credits.
This study was evaluated and approved by the ETH Zurich Ethics Commission as proposal EK-2023-N-258.

To procure an approximate number to the sample size required, an a priori power analysis was conducted in GPower (Faul et al., 2009) using the linear multiple regression (fixed model, R² deviation from zero).
text.formatted: To procure an approximate number to the sample size required, an a priori power analysis was conducted in GPower <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Faul et al., 2009)</ref> using the linear multiple regression (fixed model, R² deviation from zero).

text.text: This approach was adopted because GPower does not directly support power analyses for the planned factorial linear mixed-effects model with a factor with five levels or with two within-subject factors with two levels each.
The final analyses were conducted using linear mixed-effects models, while the G*Power analysis served solely to determine an approximate target sample size during study planning.

According to our power approximation, we aimed to collect at least fifty-three participants in order to detect a medium to large effect size f² =0.25, an α=0.05 for false positives, Power (1-β)=0.80 for the detection of a true effect, and four predictors in our most complex model.
Data were collected from seventy-four participants.

From these, seventeen participants were later excluded from the final analysis: twelve due to incomplete data files caused by technical problems during acquisition, four due to a lack of understanding or not following the instructions, and one after it was observed that the participant did not meet the inclusion criteria post-acquisition.

Consequently, the final sample size comprised fifty-seven participants, with a mean age of 22.28 (SD = 2.79) years, including twenty self-reported males, thirty-six self-reported females, and one self-reported non-binary individual.
Two virtual arm avatars were used in this experiment.
One avatar was a realistic-looking human hand and arm available for purchase at the Unity Asset Store (Storkplay, 2018).
text.formatted: One avatar was a realistic-looking human hand and arm available for purchase at the Unity Asset Store <ref type="bibr">(Storkplay, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The other avatar was a 3D model of the Hannes Hand prosthetic device (Laffranchi et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The other avatar was a 3D model of the Hannes Hand prosthetic device <ref type="bibr">(Laffranchi et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Both avatars replicated the functionality of the Hannes Hand, featuring compliant fingers that could open or close synchronously and a wrist joint that could move through a full range of motion.
Each avatar would stop when encountering an obstacle, adapting the hand's shape to the grasped object.
All virtual joints were limited to a maximal rotational speed of 450°/s to smooth the movements and avoid the feeling of teleportation between positions.
Importantly, both prosthetic avatars were used exclusively on the right arm.
To simulate a unilateral amputation of the right arm, participants wore a realistic avatar arm with unconstrained degrees of freedom in the left arm only for aesthetic purposes.
However, this left-arm avatar was not capable of interacting with the virtual environment.
The virtual environment replicated the Southampton Hand Assessment Procedure (SHAP) for assessing upper limb functionality (Cole et al., 1992).
text.formatted: The virtual environment replicated the Southampton Hand Assessment Procedure (SHAP) for assessing upper limb functionality <ref type="bibr">(Cole et al., 1992)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, it replicated the setup for the repositioning of a heavy jar task in the category of activities of daily living.
The environment included a table, a black box with a white round button, two circular areas on either side of the table, and a rectangular obstacle separating the left and right sides.
All elements within the virtual environment were scaled and positioned to mimic those used in the SHAP.

text.text: In both depictions, the virtual environment features a table, a central black box with a white button, an area for the object on the right side of the table, the object to be relocated over the right area, a relocation area on the left side, an obstacle in the middle, and a panel for providing instructions or feedback to the participant.
Information from the participant's hand was acquired through the infrared camera sensor Leap Motion Controller (Ultraleap, 2013).
text.formatted: Information from the participant's hand was acquired through the infrared camera sensor Leap Motion Controller <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Ultraleap, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The participant's wrist and forearm positions were directly transferred to the arm avatars within the virtual environment.

The closing and opening of the fingers were driven by the estimation from the Leap Motion Sensor of the degree of closure of the participant's hand, which ranged between 0 (fully open hand) and 1 (fully closed hand).

In VR, the fingers of the virtual arm avatars could not pass through objects and would stop independently upon contact, ensuring both the replication of the compliant mechanisms present in the Hannes Hand and realistic grasping behaviour.

Eye-tracking was performed with the TOBII eye tracker hardware embedded into the VIVE pro Eye virtual reality headset (HTC Corporation, 2021) inside the Unity 2021 LTS environment (Unity Technologies, 2022), with a 90Hz refresh rate, a 110° field of view, and an accuracy of 0.5°-1.1°.

The time gazing at the target object (i.e., Object-Gaze Time), the time gazing at the prosthesis (i.e., Prosthesis-Gaze Time), and the time gazing at the area on the right (i.e., Goal area-Gaze Time) were then defined as the total duration in each trial where gaze samples fell within the surface of the objects inside the VR environment.
Demographics and questionnaire data were collected via the PsyToolkit platform for the acquisition of psychological and survey data (Stoet, 2010 (Stoet, , 2017)).

text.text: The study started with a brief explanation of the experiment, followed by participants providing informed consent and the acquisition of demographic data, including age, perceived gender, level of education, perceived socioeconomic status, and handedness (Flinders Handedness survey; Nicholls et al., 2013), as well as baseline measurements assessing personality traits (Big Five Inventory-Short Form; Lang et al., 2011), cultural bias (Vertical and Horizontal Individualism and Collectivism Scale; Singelis et al., 1995), and attitude towards robots (Multi-dimensional Robot Attitude Scale; Ninomiya et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The study started with a brief explanation of the experiment, followed by participants providing informed consent and the acquisition of demographic data, including age, perceived gender, level of education, perceived socioeconomic status, and handedness (Flinders Handedness survey; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Nicholls et al., 2013)</ref>, as well as baseline measurements assessing personality traits (Big Five Inventory-Short Form; <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Lang et al., 2011)</ref>, cultural bias (Vertical and Horizontal Individualism and Collectivism Scale; <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Singelis et al., 1995)</ref>, and attitude towards robots (Multi-dimensional Robot Attitude Scale; <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Ninomiya et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These additional measures were collected as part of the broader experimental protocol but were not included in the analyses reported in the present study.
Afterwards, the participants were fitted with the VR headset, and the eye-tracker was individually calibrated.
Before starting the task, participants were introduced to the VR environments and the virtual prostheses they would use to become familiar with them.
Before each trial, participants pressed a white button aligned to their body midline, causing a white cylinder to appear on the left side.
Their task was to move or observe this cylinder moving from the left to the right circular goal area.
Subsequently, an auditory signal was generated at three different time delays (200ms, 400ms, and 600ms).
The number of delays was equally distributed among conditions, and their order was pseudorandomized.
A graphical summary of the task is presented in Figure 2.
text.formatted: A graphical summary of the task is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: The training blocks consisted of 25 trials each with sound delays of 1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds, and feedback on the delay was provided to the participant.
The experimental blocks 24 trials with sound delays of 200, 400, and 600 milliseconds, and participants were asked for their time estimation of the delay and their sense of agency over it.
Additionally, the questionnaire Prosthesis Embodiment Scale for Upper Limb Amputees (PEmbS-ULA) was administered after each experimental block.
The task structure closely followed the design in Zapparoli et al.'s prior work (2020), including 7 blocks.
The first two were designated for training and consisted of 25 trials each.
In the first training block, participants pressed a white button, causing a cylinder to move autonomously from left to right.
Subsequently, the panel displayed the precise duration of the delay between task completion and the onset of the sound stimulus.
The second training block involved participants manipulating the cylinder using a virtual arm, with the objective time delay also provided after repositioning the object, as in the previous block.
A graphical representation of the panel providing feedback about the delay's duration is presented in Figure 3.
text.formatted: A graphical representation of the panel providing feedback about the delay's duration is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: Please note that the delays during the training blocks were 1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds, while the delays during the experimental blocks were of 200, 400, and 600 milliseconds.

Since participants were not told about this manipulation, all five delay options (1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds) were available, allowing participants to select the one they perceived as appropriate if their temporal perception was influenced by the intentional binding effect.
The five experimental blocks followed, and their order was randomised across participants.

After a 500ms interval following the sound stimulus after the cylinder repositioning, a panel appeared, presenting participants with the question "How much time has passed between the end of the moving of the object and when the sound was produced?", together with five options (1ms, 200ms, 400ms, 600ms, and 800ms) for them to select as their estimation of the delay between the cylinder repositioning and the sound.

Please note that the provided delay options for 1ms and 800ms were included to allow participants to select them if they felt that was the duration of the delay due to subjective temporal compression or dilation that influenced their perception.
A graphical representation of this panel is presented in Figure 3.
text.formatted: A graphical representation of this panel is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: Participants used their head movements to select an option, with a blue dot appearing over the UI at the midline of their visual field.
Confirming the selected response requires maintaining the blue dot over the chosen option for two seconds, as indicated by a growing circular line around the dot.

Perceived temporal compression was calculated as the trial-wise difference between the reported delay and the objective delay, with more negative values indicating a stronger subjective time compression.

Upon selecting an option, another panel prompted participants to answer a slider corresponding to a visual analogue scale ranging from 0 to 100 in response to the question, "How much did you feel that the sound was produced by your movements?"
The slider ranged from "Not at all" on the left to "Entirely" on the right.
It is important to note that no numeric value was provided to the participant in this panel, neither on the scale nor for their answer.
A graphical representation of this panel is presented in Figure 3.
text.formatted: A graphical representation of this panel is presented in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>.

text.text: The five experimental blocks, each comprising 24 trials, represented distinct conditions as follows: realistic arm with slippage compensation (RS), realistic arm without slippage compensation (RF), Hannes Hand with slippage compensation (HS), Hannes Hand without slippage compensation (HF), and passive condition (P).

The participants had to reposition the cylinder themselves in every experimental block, except in the passive condition, where the cylinder moved autonomously when the white button was pressed at the beginning of each trial.

Under "without slippage compensation" conditions, participants needed to close their hand by 75% more than the initial amount required to touch the object with the thumb and another finger simultaneously to fully grasp the object.
Failure caused the object to slip with a speed proportional to the grasping between the initial grasp point and the full grasp, as if it were under the influence of gravity.
If hand closure fell below the initial grasp point, full release occurred.
In "with slippage compensation" conditions, participants secured a grasp when the thumb and at least one other finger made contact with the object.
The complete release occurred at 75% of the initial grasp point, simulating intent detection by an artificial intelligence algorithm between the states of full grasp and release.
In the first and second training blocks, as well as in the "Passive" condition, the virtual avatar alternated between the realistic avatar and the Hannes hand avatar trial-wise.
Following the completion of each of the five experimental blocks, participants were directed to look at the virtual avatar of their arm for 30 seconds, during which they could move it and operate it.
After this time, they removed the headset and responded to the sense of embodiment questionnaire (PEmbS-ULA; Bekrater-Bodmann, 2020) if the block they just completed was not the "Passive" condition.
A brief break was permitted after each block to delay the appearance of fatigue.
The overall duration of the experiment was approximately one hour.
Scores from the PEmbS-ULA were provided in the Rasch logit scale to ensure linearity within the values, according to Bekrater-Bodmann et al.

text.text: The datasets were analysed and synthesised with Python 3.6 and the Pandas package (McKinney, 2010) into a single trialwise data frame for their posterior statistical analysis.
Statistical analyses were performed in RStudio Version 2023.03.0 (RStudio Team, 2023).
text.formatted: Statistical analyses were performed in RStudio Version 2023.03.0 <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(RStudio Team, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) analyses were fitted with the R package "lme4" (Bates et al., 2014) and "lmerTest" package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) analyses were fitted with the R package "lme4" <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bates et al., 2014)</ref> and "lmerTest" package <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The participant was included as a random intercept in all LMMs to account for repeated observations.
Degrees of freedom and p-values were estimated using the Satterthwaite approximation.
Estimated marginal means were computed using the emmeans package, and pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction were performed when appropriate.
Repeated-measures analyses of variance (ANOVAs) were conducted using the afex package.
Greenhouse-Geisser corrections were applied whenever the assumption of sphericity was violated.
Significant effects were followed by pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction.
Partial eta-squared (ηp²) was reported as a measure of effect size for ANOVA results.

For intentional binding analyses, supplementary one-sample t-tests against zero were conducted at each outcome-delay level using all available activepassive differences, and Cohen's d was reported as the corresponding effect size.

Analyses were restricted to the five experimental conditions of interest: passive (P), Hannes Hand without slippage compensation (HF), Hannes Hand with slippage compensation (HS), realistic arm without slippage compensation (RF), and realistic arm with slippage compensation (RS).
The two training blocks were excluded from all the analyses.
Trials were classified as invalid if the object was not successfully repositioned using a single grasp, or if more than 50% of the object remained outside the goal area following repositioning.
Invalid trials were excluded from all subsequent analyses.
Analyses of agency measures as a function of outcome delay were adapted from Imaizumi & Tanno, (2019).
text.formatted: Analyses of agency measures as a function of outcome delay were adapted from <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Imaizumi & Tanno, (2019)</ref>.

text.text: Self-reported agency ratings were averaged across all available active and passive trials within each participant and objective-delay condition.

Unlike the original study, which considered agency ratings from active trials only, this analysis examined the overall effect of outcome delay across both task types without assessing whether this effect differed between them.
Explicit agency ratings were analysed using a one-factor repeated-measures ANOVA with objective outcome delays of 200, 400, and 600 ms as a within-subject factor.
Estimated outcome delays were averaged separately within each participant, objective-delay condition, and task type.
Estimated outcome delays were analysed using a two-factor repeated-measures ANOVA with objective outcome delay and task type (active vs. passive) as within-subject factors.

Intentional binding was calculated as the difference between estimated outcome delays in active and passive trials (active minus passive), with more negative values representing stronger subjective temporal binding.
These intentional binding scores were analysed using a one-factor repeated-measures ANOVA with objective outcome delay as a within-subject factor.

Perceived time compression at the trial level was additionally calculated as the difference between the participant's reported delay and the objective outcome delay, with more negative values representing stronger subjective temporal compression.

To examine the correspondence between self-reported agency and perceived temporal compression, a trial-wise linear mixed-effects model was fitted with self-reported agency as the outcome and perceived temporal compression as the predictor across all five experimental conditions.

To assess differences between experimental conditions, self-reported agency and perceived temporal compression were separately analysed using linear mixed-effects models with condition as a fixed effect.
To examine the effects of aesthetic appearance and motor autonomy, additional models included these factors and their interaction as fixed effects, considering only active conditions.
The same factorial structure was used to analyse prosthesis embodiment scores and object repositioning accuracy, with embodiment scores analysed at the participant-condition level.

For the analysis of the exclusion rates across active experimental conditions, trial exclusion rates were calculated at the participant level as the percentage of invalid trials within each of the active conditions: HF, HS, RF, and RS.

These exclusion rates were analysed using a linear mixed-effects model with aesthetic appearance (Hannes vs. realistic) and motor autonomy (with vs. without slippage compensation) as fixed effects and participant as a random intercept.

Separate linear mixed-effects models were fitted for prosthesis, cylinder, and goal-area dwell times across active conditions, with self-reported agency as a fixed effect and participant as a random intercept to analyse the relationship between self-reported agency and visual monitoring.
Dwell times were expressed as absolute durations in seconds.

Because nine participants contributed no valid trials in any active condition, they could not be included in analyses requiring the aesthetic appearance × motor autonomy factorial design, as the conditions analysed included only active trials.
Consequently, these analyses were restricted to 48 participants.
This restriction reflected the absence of valid active trials rather than a requirement for complete data across all four active conditions.
Similarly, One-sample tests included participants with available activepassive differences at each outcome delay, resulting in sample sizes of 43, 44, and 42 at 200, 400, and 600 ms, respectively.
The repeated-measures analyses of estimated delays and intentional binding included 37 participants with complete observations across all required task-type and delay combinations.
Analyses including passive trials retained up to 57 participants.

Appendix A provides an in-depth description and replication of the entire Results section using the subset of 48 participants with at least one valid trial in an active condition, with no significant deviations reported.

text.text: A linear mixed-effects model was fitted to examine the effect of condition on selfreported agency (explicit), with participant included as a random intercept.
The reference level was the passive condition (P), and it was based on 2,454 observations from 57 participants.
Between-participant variability (SD = 16.22) and residual variability at the trial level (SD = 16.82) were of similar magnitude.
Estimated marginal means for each condition were 37.6 (SE = 2.20) for P, 52.6 (SE = 2.43) for HF, 56.6 (SE = 2.34) for HS, 54.7 (SE = 2.44) for RF, and 57.1 (SE = 2.36) for RS.
Pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction showed significant differences among the active conditions.
Selfreported agency ratings were lower in HF than in HS (mean difference = -4.05, SE = 1.35, t(2397) = -3.00, p = .027) and in RS (mean difference = -4.56, SE = 1.39, t(2398) = -3.27, p = .011).
No other comparisons showed significant differences between active conditions.

To further characterise the effect of motor autonomy and aesthetic appearance on the sense of agency, a linear mixed-effects model was fitted to examine their effects and their interaction on self-reported agency, with participant included as a random intercept.
The model was based on 1,278 observations from 48 participants.
Betweenparticipant variability (SD = 14.70) and residual variability (SD = 16.43) were of similar magnitude.
The analysis showed a significant effect of motor autonomy.
Relative to the condition without slippage compensation (HF and RF), slippage compensation (HS and RS) was associated with higher agency ratings (β = 3.39, SE = 1.34, t(1247) = 2.52, p = .012).
In contrast, there was no significant effect of aesthetic appearance (β = 0.58, SE = 1.51, t(1244) = 0.38, p = .702).
The interaction between aesthetic appearance and autonomy was also not significant (β = -0.96, SE = 1.93, t(1240) = -0.50, p = .620).

text.text: A linear mixed-effects model was fitted to examine the relationship between selfreported agency and prosthesis dwell time, with participant included as a random intercept.

Self-reported agency was found to significantly predict prosthesis dwell time (β = -0.0014, SE = 0.0007, t(1233) = -2.13, p = .034), with higher agency ratings being associated with shorter prosthesis dwell times.
The model intercept was 0.556 (SE = 0.053, t(106) = 10.47, p < .001), indicating the predicted dwell time for self-reported agency was equal to zero.

text.text: Across all active-condition observations, the relationship between reported agency and prosthesis dwell time was negative, with an estimated slope of -0.0014.
This indicates a decrease of approximately 1.4 milliseconds in prosthesis dwell time for every one-percentage-point increase in self-reported agency.

text.text: Sharing motor autonomy with a prosthesis capable of inferring the participant's intended action was associated with higher self-reported agency and fewer failed repositioning attempts, but it did not significantly affect perceived temporal compression or prosthesis embodiment scores.
The device's aesthetic appearance did not significantly affect or moderate sense of agency measures, nor did it significantly affect prosthesis embodiment.
Additionally, shorter outcome delays were associated with higher self-reported agency, whereas intentional binding increased in absolute magnitude at longer delays.
Lastly, higher self-reported agency was associated with shorter dwell times over the prosthesis and the object being manipulated.
The analysis of perceived temporal compression and self-reported agency measures found a significant correlation between explicit and implicit measures of the sense of agency.

This finding is consistent with previous studies reporting associations between explicit judgments of agency and intentional binding measures (Ebert & Wegner, 2010; Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019; Schofield et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This finding is consistent with previous studies reporting associations between explicit judgments of agency and intentional binding measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Ebert & Wegner, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Schofield et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: To the best of our knowledge, only a limited number of studies have investigated the sense of agency over upper-limb prostheses using an implicit agency paradigm, with Schofield et al. (2019) providing the most directly comparable example.
text.formatted: To the best of our knowledge, only a limited number of studies have investigated the sense of agency over upper-limb prostheses using an implicit agency paradigm, with <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Schofield et al. (2019)</ref> providing the most directly comparable example.

text.text: In contrast to the open-ended temporal estimates used in previous work (Schofield et al., 2019), the present study employed a fixedresponse time estimation paradigm, supporting the use of this paradigm for the measurement of implicit sense of agency in tasks employing an upper limb prosthesis.
text.formatted: In contrast to the open-ended temporal estimates used in previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Schofield et al., 2019)</ref>, the present study employed a fixedresponse time estimation paradigm, supporting the use of this paradigm for the measurement of implicit sense of agency in tasks employing an upper limb prosthesis.

text.text: Additionally, the analysis of the effect of objective outcome delay (200 ms, 400 ms, and 600 ms) on self-reported agency revealed significant differences across all delay conditions, with higher agency ratings associated with shorter delays.

This decrease in explicitly reported agency in the present study is consistent with previous research demonstrating that the sense of agency decreases as the temporal interval between an action and its outcome increases (Erdoğan & Balcı, 2025; Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019; Kim & Yoshida, 2024).
text.formatted: This decrease in explicitly reported agency in the present study is consistent with previous research demonstrating that the sense of agency decreases as the temporal interval between an action and its outcome increases <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Erdoğan & Balcı, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Kim & Yoshida, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such effects have been attributed to a weakening of the perceived causal relationship between an action and its consequence as temporal contiguity decreases, reducing the likelihood that the outcome is attributed to one's own action (Wen & Imamizu, 2022).
text.formatted: Such effects have been attributed to a weakening of the perceived causal relationship between an action and its consequence as temporal contiguity decreases, reducing the likelihood that the outcome is attributed to one's own action <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Wen & Imamizu, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, significant intentional binding effects were observed at all delay levels, indicating the presence of intentional binding at delays longer than those commonly observed in previous studies (Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019; Zapparoli et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Similarly, significant intentional binding effects were observed at all delay levels, indicating the presence of intentional binding at delays longer than those commonly observed in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Zapparoli et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This was not expected and may relate to the embodied nature and temporal structure of our task.

Unlike the discrete action used by Zapparoli et al. (2020), the present task involved a prolonged sequence of grasping, transporting, and releasing an object, accompanied by continuous visuomotor feedback.
text.formatted: Unlike the discrete action used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Zapparoli et al. (2020)</ref>, the present task involved a prolonged sequence of grasping, transporting, and releasing an object, accompanied by continuous visuomotor feedback.

text.text: These features may have contributed to the observed binding pattern, although the present design does not allow their individual contributions to be isolated.
However, the magnitude of intentional binding increased in absolute duration in longer delays, with the strongest effect observed at 600 ms.
Notably, this pattern contrasted with the explicit agency ratings, which decreased as outcome delay increased.
Thus, increasing action-outcome delays produced opposite effects on explicit and implicit measures of agency.

This dissociation may reflect differences in the processes underlying the two measures: explicit judgments may rely more strongly on conscious causal attribution, whereas intentional binding may be influenced by temporal prediction and retrospective outcome processing.

This interpretation is consistent with the evidence suggesting that the two measures may capture partially distinct aspects of agency processing (Ciaunica et al., 2024; Erdoğan & Balcı, 2025; Reddy, 2022).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with the evidence suggesting that the two measures may capture partially distinct aspects of agency processing <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ciaunica et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Erdoğan & Balcı, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Reddy, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, we cannot discard that the increase in the intentional binding effect as outcome delay increased may also have been influenced by Weber's law, which states that the just noticeable difference between two intervals is known to be proportional to the standard interval (Erdoğan & Balcı, 2025).
text.formatted: However, we cannot discard that the increase in the intentional binding effect as outcome delay increased may also have been influenced by Weber's law, which states that the just noticeable difference between two intervals is known to be proportional to the standard interval <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Erdoğan & Balcı, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: A possible explanation would be that the use of a fixed 200 ms step difference between adjacent delays, together with the decrease in perceptual discrimination with delay magnitude, may have increased the likelihood that participants perceived delays as differing by more than a single interval.

Under this explanation, reduced temporal discrimination would need to interact with agency-related perceived temporal compression differently in active and passive trials to account for the increasing difference between them as objective delay increased.

Although this explanation remains speculative, future studies should address the exploration of how the use of constant, linearly spaced delays in complex motor tasks interacts with delay magnitude and outcome expectations, both of which have been associated with effects on subjective time perception (Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019; Mariano et al., 2025; Tanaka et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Although this explanation remains speculative, future studies should address the exploration of how the use of constant, linearly spaced delays in complex motor tasks interacts with delay magnitude and outcome expectations, both of which have been associated with effects on subjective time perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Mariano et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tanaka et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Analysis of the effect of sharing the motor autonomy of the prosthetic device with an intention-detection algorithm indicated a positive effect on both self-reported (explicit) sense of agency over the device and the reduction in the number of failed repositioning attempts, with a trend toward improved placement accuracy.
These findings support our hypothesis that an intention-detection algorithm could reduce the number of grasping failures while using a prosthetic device.

Previous work has linked increased grasping failures to reduced explicit agency (Egle et al., 2026), suggesting that the reduced failure rate observed in this study may have contributed to the increase in agency ratings.
text.formatted: Previous work has linked increased grasping failures to reduced explicit agency <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Egle et al., 2026)</ref>, suggesting that the reduced failure rate observed in this study may have contributed to the increase in agency ratings.

text.text: Shared autonomy may therefore enhance agency when it supports the intended action without removing the user's contribution to its execution.
Future studies could examine this hypothesis by testing whether grasping failure rates mediate the effect of shared motor autonomy on explicit agency.
Interestingly, no differences in prosthesis embodiment scores were found among conditions.

Although this result does not support a direct relationship between the increased sense of agency and greater device embodiment, it suggests that agency alone may not be sufficient to produce a broader experience of embodiment.
Other components, such as ownership, anatomical plausibility, and multisensory integration, may require longer exposure to the device.
Nevertheless, these results need to be interpreted with caution, as the PEmbS-ULA scale was developed to assess the clinical population with amputation rather than the able-bodied population.
Therefore, it is possible that embodiment processes in able-bodied participants differ from those in individuals with limb loss.

In particular, previous work on the Rubber Hand Illusion has shown that embodiment of an artificial limb can be accompanied by partial disownership of the biological limb (della Gatta et al., 2016), potentially complicating the interpretation of embodiment scores in able-bodied samples.
text.formatted: In particular, previous work on the Rubber Hand Illusion has shown that embodiment of an artificial limb can be accompanied by partial disownership of the biological limb <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(della Gatta et al., 2016)</ref>, potentially complicating the interpretation of embodiment scores in able-bodied samples.

text.text: Additionally, our study design limits each virtual avatar's use to a few minutes within a constrained interaction environment, potentially limiting the integration of the prosthesis as part of the bodily self.

However, despite a clear difference in the magnitude of perceived temporal compression between the active and passive conditions, motor autonomy did not significantly affect the implicit measure of agency.
In contrast, self-reported agency ratings were significantly influenced by motor autonomy.

This dissociation suggests that implicit and explicit measures of agency may be differentially sensitive to changes in prosthesis autonomy, consistent with previous evidence showing that the two measures can respond differently depending on the task and experimental context (Ciaunica et al., 2024; Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019).
text.formatted: This dissociation suggests that implicit and explicit measures of agency may be differentially sensitive to changes in prosthesis autonomy, consistent with previous evidence showing that the two measures can respond differently depending on the task and experimental context <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ciaunica et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Imaizumi & Tanno, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the aesthetic appearance of the device did not significantly affect or moderate the explicit or the implicit sense of agency, nor prosthesis embodiment.
These findings suggest that, within the context of the present task, functional aspects of the interaction may have had a greater influence than visual appearance.
Indeed, because both avatars provided comparable visuomotor correspondence, differences in appearance may have been less relevant than the reliability of action execution.

However, it would be necessary to further explore this effect in the population of prosthetic users, as personalisation and human-likeness of prosthetic devices have been found to be relevant for their embodiment and acceptance (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2020 , 2021; Caldas et al., 2026).
text.formatted: However, it would be necessary to further explore this effect in the population of prosthetic users, as personalisation and human-likeness of prosthetic devices have been found to be relevant for their embodiment and acceptance <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bekrater-Bodmann, 2020</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Caldas et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The virtual setting may also have contributed to the limited influence of aesthetic appearance observed in this study.

Previous studies have shown ownership of virtual limbs with substantially altered proportions when congruent sensorimotor feedback was provided (Kilteni et al., 2012), and found that movement congruency influenced intentional binding regardless of whether the controlled virtual object resembled a hand (Zopf et al., 2018), which may support the idea that consistent sensorimotor feedback can support aspects of agency and embodiment despite visual differences.
text.formatted: Previous studies have shown ownership of virtual limbs with substantially altered proportions when congruent sensorimotor feedback was provided <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Kilteni et al., 2012)</ref>, and found that movement congruency influenced intentional binding regardless of whether the controlled virtual object resembled a hand <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Zopf et al., 2018)</ref>, which may support the idea that consistent sensorimotor feedback can support aspects of agency and embodiment despite visual differences.

text.text: Lastly, the analysis of the gaze behaviour showed a decrease in the dwell times over the prosthesis and task object as the sense of agency increased.
These results support our hypothesis that a higher sense of agency over the device would be associated with reduced visual monitoring of it.
Evidence supporting this claim has also been found in terms of trust, reliability, and sense of control over the prosthetic device (Cheng et al., 2025; Egle et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Evidence supporting this claim has also been found in terms of trust, reliability, and sense of control over the prosthetic device <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cheng et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Egle et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: It is important to acknowledge that the findings of this study are constrained by several limitations.
First, our experiment was conducted on a sample of able-bodied young adults.

Although direct evidence comparing prosthesis embodiment between ablebodied and limb-missing individuals remains limited, sense of embodiment is generally considered to be mediated by the internal representation of the limb (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2020), which may undergo changes following amputation (Makin & Flor, 2020).
text.formatted: Although direct evidence comparing prosthesis embodiment between ablebodied and limb-missing individuals remains limited, sense of embodiment is generally considered to be mediated by the internal representation of the limb (Bekrater-Bodmann, 2020), which may undergo changes following amputation <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Makin & Flor, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Second, movements of the virtual prosthesis were controlled using kinematic information obtained by optical hand tracking rather than from electromyography (EMG) signals.

EMG control in polyarticulated prosthetic devices is more prone to movement misclassifications (Alotaibi et al., 2023), what has been associated with a decrease in the trust in, and sense of agency over, prosthetic devices (Egle et al., 2026).
text.formatted: EMG control in polyarticulated prosthetic devices is more prone to movement misclassifications <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Alotaibi et al., 2023)</ref>, what has been associated with a decrease in the trust in, and sense of agency over, prosthetic devices <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Egle et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the simulated intention-detection algorithm used represents an ideal system, as it had direct access to the participant's real hand state to adapt its behaviour, potentially increasing its accuracy with respect to a real inference algorithm.
Third, prosthesis embodiment was assessed using the PEmbS-ULA, a questionnaire validated for individuals with an upper-limb amputation.
Although it provides a useful framework for evaluating sense of embodiment, its psychometric properties have not been established for able-bodied participants interacting with virtual prostheses.

Lastly, this study was conducted in a single session inside a VR environment and, as a result, it may not capture longer-term changes in embodiment arising from prolonged prosthesis use, nor from the haptic experiences associated with interacting with physical prosthetic devices in complex everyday environments.
Future studies should aim to mitigate the limitations of this study and further validate its results across different tasks outside a VR environment using real physical prosthetic devices.
In conclusion, our study explored factors influencing the sense of agency and embodiment of a virtual prosthesis in a VR environment.
The results showed that sharing autonomy with an ideal intention-detection algorithm can enhance self-reported agency while improving task performance by reducing grasping failures.

Despite the correlation between explicit and implicit measures of agency, they responded differently to outcome delay and motor autonomy, supporting the view that they capture related yet partially distinct aspects of the sense of agency.

Contrary to our expectations, motor autonomy and the prosthesis's aesthetic appearance did not significantly affect embodiment, suggesting that functional aspects of the interaction may have a greater influence than visual appearance during short-term use in our population.

Finally, the observed association between higher self-reported agency and reduced visual attention toward the prosthesis and manipulated object provided further insight into the effect of agency over the prosthesis on gaze behaviour.

Together, these findings contribute to our understanding of the sense of agency in prosthetic devices and highlight the potential of shared-autonomy approaches to improve the experience of upper-limb prosthesis users, warranting further investigation in clinical populations.

Figure2.
Graphical summary of the experimental task.

The task would be composed of seven blocks: two for training in sequence (Passive and Active) and five experimental blocks in a pseudo-randomised order (realistic arm with slippage compensation (RS), realistic arm without slippage compensation (RF), Hannes Hand with slippage compensation (HS), Hannes Hand without slippage compensation (HF), and passive condition (P)).
The training blocks consisted of 25 trials each with sound delays of 1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds, and feedback on the delay was provided to the participant.
The experimental blocks 24 trials with sound delays of 200, 400, and 600 milliseconds, and participants were asked for their time estimation of the delay and their sense of agency over it.
Additionally, the questionnaire Prosthesis Embodiment Scale for Upper Limb Amputees (PEmbS-ULA) was administered after each experimental block.
Figure3.

Graphical representation of the panel providing feedback about the delay's duration during the training blocks (left of the black line) and of the panels used during the experimental blocks (right of the black line) to estimate the duration of the delay (centre) and their level of self-reported agency (right).
Please note that the delays during the training blocks were 1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds, while the delays during the experimental blocks were of 200, 400, and 600 milliseconds.

Since participants were not told about this manipulation, all five delay options (1, 200, 400, 600, and 800 milliseconds) were available, allowing participants to select the one they perceived as appropriate if their temporal perception was influenced by the intentional binding effect.
